title: Rereading chapters 17–20
hook: reread anger, impurity, the just, the way
tomorrow: why does a craving grow like a vine, and what slows it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two readings of love nothing: let go of everything, or let go of the grip. Both kept one thing: happier now, holding dear things lightly. Today, a sound from a workshop.

Polishing a tarnished ring always takes longer than it should. Rub, look, rub again. The dark comes off a little at a time, never all at once. The Dhammapada's chapter on impurity has a craftsman doing something like it, and the sound is breath. A smith bends over silver and blows. Not one big gust. A steady breath, and another, and another.
screen: `A TARNISHED RING.` → `RUB, LOOK, RUB AGAIN.` → `A SMITH BLOWS ON SILVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in Max Müller's translation: “Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.” Read it with your ears. One by one. Little by little. From time to time. Three phrases, and none of them says now, all of it, done. Reread, the four chapters around this verse all sound like that workshop. The chapter on anger gives a driver, not a saint: “He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.” Holding back is an action you repeat, every time the chariot rolls. The chapter on the just says a person isn't learned because they talk a lot; the one who is patient, free of hatred and fear, is the learned one. Patience again: a slow skill. Then the chapter on the way puts the work in your own hands: “You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers.” The Buddhas point. The walking is yours. So the carry today isn't arrived, or clean, or fixed. It's on the way. The silver brightens under each breath, and the smith keeps breathing.
screen: `ONE BY ONE, LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · `THE REAL DRIVER HOLDS BACK ANGER.` · `LEARNED MEANS PATIENT.` · `YOU WALK IT YOURSELF.` · then, large: `ON THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Breathe out slowly through softly pursed lips, the way a smith might blow on silver: long, steady, never forced. Let the in-breath come back on its own. With each slow breath out, let one small thing loosen, an irritation from this morning, a tight jaw, and keep the rhythm going until the bell.
Rereading chapters 17 to 20: anger, impurity, the just and the way, read again. Four chapters that all work like a smith's breath: little by little.
Carry this: on the way, one breath on the silver at a time. Day five of the reread.

howItsDone: Buddhist meditation often takes the breath as its object, as the Anapanasati Sutta teaches, and teachers speak of the path as gradual training, returned to day after day.

fork.setup: your dad is trying to stop snapping at people when he's tired. he slipped twice this week and says he's failed. what does the smith verse say?
options: he's on the way: it clears little by little, from time to time.
two slips this week show the habit is just who he is now.
he should wait until he feels calmer before trying again.
fork.reveal: the verse never promises one clean sweep. one by one, little by little: a slip is the next breath on the silver, not the end of the work.

original.note: Pali: path, way; the twentieth chapter is the Maggavagga, the chapter on the way.

what a scholar hears: verse 239 in the Malavagga (impurity) pairs well with 276 in the Maggavagga: the effort is one's own; Tathāgata, 'thus-gone', is a name for a Buddha.

chat.says: trying to get ông's hands right for the big piece. redrew them 9 times. about to quit.
options: keep going, little by little. each pass clears a bit, like the smith's breath.
nine tries and still wrong means hands just aren't your thing. skip them.
start a totally new piece; fresh ideas beat fixing an old drawing.
chat.meaning: Dhammapada 239: the wise clear their faults as a smith clears silver, one by one, little by little. Nine passes isn't failure; it's the way.

tie.story: The smith in the Dhammapada blows the impurities off silver one by one, little by little.
